## Contents. # NEMA contact ratings. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia. **NEMA contact ratings** are how much current at a rated voltage a relay or other pilot device can switch. The current rating of smaller NEMA contactors or their auxiliaries are defined by *NEMA ICS 5: Industrial Control and Systems, Control Circuit and Pilot Devices* standard. The nomenclature is a letter followed by a three-digit number, the letter designates the current rating of the contacts and the current type (i.e., AC or DC) and the number designates the maximum voltage design values. ## AC Contact Ratings. | Contact Rating Designation | Thermal Current | Voltage |. ## DC Contact Ratings. | Contact Rating Designation | Thermal Current | Voltage | Voltamperes |. ## References. 1. **^** "NEMA ICS 5-2017".

The International electrotechnical commission in their standard for low voltage switchgear (IEC 60947) as well as in their standard for safety requirements for Solid State Relays (IEC 62314) has defined utilization categories to simplify the selection of devices.*. –**IEC 60947-4-3** : AC semiconductor controllers and contactors for non motor loads. **All our Solid State Relays & Contactors are characterized by the utilization category together with the rated operational voltage and current indicated.**. Therefore, in our data-sheets we specify both AC-1 and AC-3 rated currents for products suitable for all kinds of loads. For example, if we declare that a Solid State Contactor has an AC-3 rated current of 16A at 400V means that this contactor can control motors with a maximum rated current of 16A at 400V (when mounted on a proper heatsink). The two main types of ratings that are used for Solid State Relays & Contactors are AC-1 / LC A and AC-3 / LC B.

Keep in mind that the number of NEMA contactors (8) available from 1 to 200hp as compared to the number of IEC contactors (15) in some cases require an oversized NEMA device for the application adding unnecessary additional cost and size. Typically, IEC devices rated above 30A (and 9A through 30A contactor from some manufacturers) have replacement contact kits to extend the electrical life of the contactor. The motor’s size (HP) often guides starter selection, especially for NEMA-rated starters which are chosen by HP and voltage. For instance, NEMA starters inherently have this margin – a NEMA Size 3 starter is rated for 90 A continuous and covers motors up to 50 HP @ 460 V. Safety means all components (wires, starter, overload, upstream fuse/breaker) are coordinated: the wiring can carry the current (sized ≥125% FLC), the short-circuit protection will clear faults without destroying the starter, and the overload will protect the motor from long-term overheating. You don’t need to calculate exact FLA or duty cycle – if the motor’s HP is within a size’s range, that starter will work (including handling the start current). For example, using a NEMA Size 4 starter on a motor that only needs a Size 2: the Size 4’s overload range might be too high to even set properly for the small motor, or someone might leave the overload at a default high setting, defeating the protection.

Keep in mind that the number of NEMA contactors (8) available from 1 to 200hp as compared to the number of IEC contactors (15) in some cases require an oversized NEMA device for the application adding unnecessary additional cost and size. Equivalently rated IEC contactors (9A to 100A) typically provide a mechanical life of 10 million to 15 million operations. Typically, IEC devices rated above 30A (and 9A through 30A contactor from some manufacturers) have replacement contact kits to extend the electrical life of the contactor. Although there are differences in NEMA-rated contactors versus their IEC-rated counterparts, those differences are not justified when used in the manufacture of bypasses for variable frequency drives from a practical life, serviceability and, most importantly, cost viewpoint.

# Electrical Contactor Ratings Explained: Voltage, Current, and Applications. Contactor ratings exist to define the conditions under which a device can operate safely and reliably. A CHINT contactor, like other IEC-compliant devices, clearly separates its ratings by load type, voltage, and duty cycle so users can make informed decisions rather than relying on guesswork. Rated operational current, or Ie, specifies the maximum current a contactor can carry under defined conditions. The same contactor may have different current ratings depending on the type of load it controls. Mechanical endurance refers to how many operations the contactor can perform with no electrical load, while electrical endurance reflects how many operations it can handle under rated load conditions. Choosing the right contactor means matching its ratings to real operating conditions rather than relying on a single current or voltage value. Whether you are specifying new equipment or maintaining existing systems, a clear understanding of contactor ratings, illustrated through examples like a CHINT contactor, provides a strong foundation for safe and effective electrical control.

The International electrotechnical commission in their standard for low voltage switchgear (IEC 60947) as well as in their standard for safety requirements for Solid State Relays (IEC 62314) has defined utilization categories to simplify the selection of devices.*. –**IEC 60947-4-3** : AC semiconductor controllers and contactors for non motor loads. **All our Solid State Relays & Contactors are characterized by the utilization category together with the rated operational voltage and current indicated.**. Therefore, in our data-sheets we specify both AC-1 and AC-3 rated currents for products suitable for all kinds of loads. For example, if we declare that a Solid State Contactor has an AC-3 rated current of 16A at 400V means that this contactor can control motors with a maximum rated current of 16A at 400V (when mounted on a proper heatsink). The two main types of ratings that are used for Solid State Relays & Contactors are AC-1 / LC A and AC-3 / LC B.

The International electrotechnical commission in their standard for low voltage switchgear (IEC 60947) as well as in their standard for safety requirements for Solid State Relays (IEC 62314) has defined utilization categories to simplify the selection of devices.*. –**IEC 60947-4-3** : AC semiconductor controllers and contactors for non motor loads. **All our Solid State Relays & Contactors are characterized by the utilization category together with the rated operational voltage and current indicated.**. Therefore, in our data-sheets we specify both AC-1 and AC-3 rated currents for products suitable for all kinds of loads. For example, if we declare that a Solid State Contactor has an AC-3 rated current of 16A at 400V means that this contactor can control motors with a maximum rated current of 16A at 400V (when mounted on a proper heatsink). The two main types of ratings that are used for Solid State Relays & Contactors are AC-1 / LC A and AC-3 / LC B.

# Clearing Up the Confusion Between NEMA and IEC Contactors. This is certainly the case with respect to industrial motor control devices that adhere to standards from either the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) or the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) in Europe. While this is certainly not a new issue – it dates back to the late 1980s – I find customers are often still confused about the differences between NEMA- and IEC-compatible controllers, and when to use one vs. If a customer or contractor needs a NEMA size 2 contactor, he can pick one off a shelf from any number of suppliers with confidence it will be suitable for an appropriately rated motor. # Electrical Contactor Ratings Explained: Voltage, Current, and Applications. Contactor ratings exist to define the conditions under which a device can operate safely and reliably. A CHINT contactor, like other IEC-compliant devices, clearly separates its ratings by load type, voltage, and duty cycle so users can make informed decisions rather than relying on guesswork. Rated operational current, or Ie, specifies the maximum current a contactor can carry under defined conditions. The same contactor may have different current ratings depending on the type of load it controls. Mechanical endurance refers to how many operations the contactor can perform with no electrical load, while electrical endurance reflects how many operations it can handle under rated load conditions. Choosing the right contactor means matching its ratings to real operating conditions rather than relying on a single current or voltage value. Whether you are specifying new equipment or maintaining existing systems, a clear understanding of contactor ratings, illustrated through examples like a CHINT contactor, provides a strong foundation for safe and effective electrical control.

Both NEMA and IEC motor starters and contactors have nameplates (labels) that list ratings to help the user select and apply the devices. NEMA Size: A standardized rating system of sizes for motor controllers. Rated Operational Current (Ie): The maximum FLC at which a motor starter or contactor may be used for a given combination of voltage, frequency, and utilization category (AC-1, AC-3, etc). Since the installer often orders a controller by the motor horsepower and voltage rating, and may not know the application or duty cycle planned for the motor and its controller, the NEMA contactor is designed by convention with sufficient reserve capacity to assure performance over a broad band of applications without the need for an assessment of life requirements. IEC contactors used in the U.S. are usually marked with voltage values (Ue) and with Horsepower (or Kilowatt) ratings, for use with the maximum AC-3 rated operational current (le). The IEC test for AC-3 is set up so that the contacts make six times the motor full load current (FLC) at the full rated voltage....

## Contents. # NEMA contact ratings. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia. **NEMA contact ratings** are how much current at a rated voltage a relay or other pilot device can switch. The current rating of smaller NEMA contactors or their auxiliaries are defined by *NEMA ICS 5: Industrial Control and Systems, Control Circuit and Pilot Devices* standard. # Electrical Contactor Ratings Explained: Voltage, Current, and Applications. Contactor ratings exist to define the conditions under which a device can operate safely and reliably. A CHINT contactor, like other IEC-compliant devices, clearly separates its ratings by load type, voltage, and duty cycle so users can make informed decisions rather than relying on guesswork. Rated operational current, or Ie, specifies the maximum current a contactor can carry under defined conditions. The same contactor may have different current ratings depending on the type of load it controls. Mechanical endurance refers to how many operations the contactor can perform with no electrical load, while electrical endurance reflects how many operations it can handle under rated load conditions. Choosing the right contactor means matching its ratings to real operating conditions rather than relying on a single current or voltage value. Whether you are specifying new equipment or maintaining existing systems, a clear understanding of contactor ratings, illustrated through examples like a CHINT contactor, provides a strong foundation for safe and effective electrical control.

Equivalently rated IEC contactors (9A to 100A) typically provide a mechanical life of 10 million to 15 million operations. Typically, IEC devices rated above 30A (and 9A through 30A contactor from some manufacturers) have replacement contact kits to extend the electrical life of the contactor. NEMA contact ratings are how much current at a rated voltage a relay or other pilot device can switch. The current rating of smaller NEMA contactors or their auxiliaries are defined by NEMA ICS 5: Industrial Control and Systems, Control Circuit and Pilot Devices standard. The nomenclature is a letter followed by a three-digit number, the letter designates the current rating of the contacts and the current type (i.e., AC or DC) and the number designates the maximum voltage design values.

Eaton XT IEC Power Control Family | XT Series — Reversing & Non-reversing Vacuum Contactors | Power Control 580 to 2600 A:

The XT ICE Series contactors use an electronic coil interface design that allows for flexibility in switching and greater reliability. These high-amperage contactors can be switched conventionally with full power to the coil, directly from a PLC output, or from a low-power command device. Low pickup and sealing power generates less heat and reduces the investment in control power transformers. The three switching tubes and electromechanical drive system of the XT 580–2600A contactors are arranged in an extremely compact design. This allows for smaller switchgear dimensions, while switching higher currents—up to 2600A.The XT IEC series includes non-reversing and reversing contactors and starters as well as overload relays and accessories. Enclosed control options include metallic and non-metallic enclosures with circuit breakers, and North American or European fuses. The XT line of IEC motor control is not the same as traditional motor control designs. XT was designed to be engineered better.

Family Features:
  • Toolless assembly of manual motor controllers and reversing contactors
  • Low coil consumption
  • Front accessibility to coil terminations
  • Built-in surge suppression on electronic coils
  • Built-in auxiliary contact for contactors up to 32A in a 45 mm frame
  • Finger-safe and back-of-hand proof ratings
  • Direct PLC control on 185A–2000A contactors

    The XT Family line includes a large offering of power control components and accessories that cover a broad range of applications and ratings:
  • Three-pole contactors to 2000A
  • Four-pole contactors to 200A
  • Capacitor contactors to 680 kVAR
  • Mini contactors to 9A
  • Relays to 16A
  • Thermal overload relays to 630A
  • Electronic overload relays to 1500A
  • Manual motor protectors to 65A
  • Manual motor controllers and combination motor controllers to 65A

    Additional Information:
    — Electronic coil controller allows contactors to reduce power consumption and generate less heat, resulting in lower cooling requirements, the ability to mount more contactors/starters per cabinet, and an extended life on pilot devices that carry control signals.
    — AC and DC devices with the same dimensions achieved with an electronically controlled coil system allow for space savings and reduced engineering design time.
    — Integrated suppressors in DC controlled contactors offers reductions in total logistics and inventory costs by limiting the number of products ordered and stocked.
    — Wiring is not required, therefore increasing installation and maintenance efficiency.
    — Expanded range of DC coil control voltages, allows reliable operation through fluctuations in control voltages.
    — Twin terminals with separate sockets in contactors up to 400A offer installation and application flexibility when using different size wires. The improved integrity of the connections reduces cabling faults.
